svg.text: Only height 1 lets G stop running at low energy
log10 a (a = 1/g; large a = low energy, G nearly constant)
rate at that point, V_s(a) / a
s = 1: V(a) = 1 + a, rate → 1 exactly
What this shows
At low energy, G is a constant and
g = G k² grows exactly like k².
That needs a fixed rate at a = ∞.
s = 1 settles to 1.
s = 1.1 (the fitted height) keeps
climbing, slowly, like a log.
s < 1 sinks to 0, s > 1 climbs.
At the other end, the wall E^s(−∞),
the rate is 1 for every s (check H8).
So the height can't make the two
ends' rates differ by 23/22.
It only spoils the low-energy end.
Curves are ours: V_s(a) = (E^s)′(E^−s(a)) is the rate of the height-s law B_s(a, b) = E^s(E^−s a + E^−s b), computed by regular iteration.
Rescaling to (1/k) B_s(ka, kb) multiplies both end rates by k, so the ratio is unchanged (check H10). Checks H7–H10.
